<meta>continues from previous page: the debate between Mozi and Gongmengzi on whether ghosts and spirits can send fortune and misfortune</meta>cannot bring about misfortune or good fortune; they hold that there is neither the auspicious nor the inauspicious. That is why government falls into disorder and the state is endangered. So it is that the books of the former kings, in the <term>Ziyi</term> <gloss>a section of the ancient documents, as the text here names it</gloss>, also have this: "Its arrogance comes from you, and it is inauspicious." <note>丌: the old editions all write this character as 亓, an archaic form of 其, "its."</note> This means that doing what is not good brings punishment, and doing what is good brings reward.

Master Mozi said to Gongmengzi: "By the rites of mourning, when a ruler, a father or mother, a wife, or the eldest son <insert>the heir son</insert> dies, three years are spent in mourning dress; for paternal uncles and brothers, and for clansmen, five months; for father's sisters, elder sisters, mother's brothers, and sisters' sons, there are mourning periods of several months each. <note>The received text gives a one-year mourning for uncles and brothers and five months for clansmen; the transcription here runs these together.</note> Or, in the intervals when not in mourning, people chant the three hundred Odes, play the three hundred Odes on strings, sing the three hundred Odes, and dance the three hundred Odes. <note>The "three hundred Odes" are the poems of the Classic of Poetry (Shijing), which the Confucians recited, set to music, sang, and danced as part of ritual training.</note> If we followed your words, on what day would the gentleman attend to government, and on what day would the common people pursue their work?"

Gongmengzi said: "When the state is in disorder, one puts it in order; when it is in order, one practices rites and music. When the state is in order, one pursues work; when the state is wealthy, one practices rites and music." <note>The received text reads "when the state is poor, one pursues work"; the transcription here has "in order" in place of "poor."</note>

Master Mozi said: "The order of a state <insert>Lu Wenchao says that five characters, "is ordered because it is governed," have dropped out below this point</insert>: if governing is abandoned, then the order of the state is abandoned too. The state's

<summary>In this passage from the "Gongmeng" chapter of the Mozi, Mozi cites the ancient books to show that bad conduct brings punishment and good conduct reward, then attacks the Confucian burden of long mourning periods and constant ritual music. When Gongmengzi replies that rites and music belong to times of order and wealth, Mozi begins to answer that order lasts only as long as the work of governing continues.</summary>
<keywords>Mozi, Gongmengzi, Confucians, mourning rites, three-year mourning, Classic of Poetry, three hundred Odes, rites and music, government, reward and punishment, ghosts and spirits, auspicious and inauspicious, Lu Wenchao, textual commentary</keywords>
